images.filename: Biblioteca Vasconcelos, Ciudad de México, México, 2015-07-20, DD 16-18 HDR.JPG
images.caption: Biblioteca Vasconcelos (Vasconcelos Library) is a library located in the north of Mexico City, Mexico. Inaugurated in 2006, it had 600,000 publications and books by 2015, though there are plans to host up to 2 million items. The building has a surface area of about 38,000 square metres (410,000 sq ft), and was visited by 1.7 million people in 2014; it can host 5,000 people at the same time.

images.caption: Painting of different combinations of races according to the Casta system. There are 16 images of the races in a grid, then a 17th of Indigenous people before colonization surrounded by nature. The text reads Español + India - Mestizo or Cholo, Español + Mestiza - Castizo or cuarterón, Castizo + Española - Español Criollo, Negro + Española - Mulato, Mulato + Española - Morisco, Morisco + Española - Albina, Español + Tornatrás Negro, Torna atrás + India - Lobo o Zambo, Indio + Loba - Chino, Chino + India - Zambaiga, Zambaiga + Chino - Cambujo, Cambuja + Chino - Genízara, Genízara + Chino - Albarazado, Albarazado + Negra - Calpamula, Calpamula + Albarazado - Gíbaro, Gíbaro + Albarazao - Tente en el aire, Mecos and Mecas, even though they are many, they are all similar.
images.alt: Painting of different combinations of races according to the Casta system. There are 16 images of the races in a grid, then a 17th of Indigenous people before colonization surrounded by nature. The text reads Español + India - Mestizo or Cholo, Español + Mestiza - Castizo or cuarterón, Castizo + Española - Español Criollo, Negro + Española - Mulato, Mulato + Española - Morisco, Morisco + Española - Albina, Español + Tornatrás Negro, Torna atrás + India - Lobo o Zambo, Indio + Loba - Chino, Chino + India - Zambaiga, Zambaiga + Chino - Cambujo, Cambuja + Chino - Genízara, Genízara + Chino - Albarazado, Albarazado + Negra - Calpamula, Calpamula + Albarazado - Gíbaro, Gíbaro + Albarazao - Tente en el aire, Mecos and Mecas, even though they are many, they are all similar.

images.caption:
Hablando de dilapidar herencias:
Al preguntársele qué pensaba de las reformas en materia energética que PRI-PAN pretenden imponer a Pemex, Cuauhtémoc dio una declaración muy rara:
"He escuchado declaraciones de altos funcionarios del gobierno federal en el sentido de que no se privatizará Pemex así que no creo que pase. Estoy de acuerdo con que pueda haber inversiones privadas para su modernización".
Quien fuera candidato presidencial de la Izquierda y Jefe de Gobierno del Distrito Federal, hijo de Lázaro Cárdenas y líder moral del PRD, ahora confía ciégamente en la buena fe y la palabra de los altos funcionarios priistas. 

Seguramente esto es sintomático del vacío de ideales que ha afectado al partido del sol en los últimos meses.

images.filename: Daniel del Valle, Moctezuma II Museo Nacional De Arte.jpg
images.caption:
Painting made by Mexican artist Daniel del Valle titled Moctezuma II visitando las tumbas de sus antepasados (Moctezuma II visiting the tombs of his ancestors), made in 1895 and currently located at the National Museum of Art in Mexico City, oil on canvas. The painting depicts Moctezuma II, Emperor of the Mexica Empire, visiting the engravings on the stones of the forest of Chapultepec (in modern-day Mexico City) depicting the previous Emperors. Nowadays, only Moctezuma's engraving has partially survived, the rest being destroyed during the Mexican Colonial Period.
This painting is Daniel del Valle's most notable work, through which the artist "went down in history", being made during a period in the 19th century in which Mexican artists participated in the search of the national identity through the abundant creation historical works, such as monuments, lithographs and paintings. Through this search, the pre-Hispanic past of the country was given its lost value to affirm the Mexican nationality.

This particular work was the winner of a competition held in 1895 by the National School of Fine Arts, in the Academy of San Carlos. Del Valle received the work's theme from Master José Salomé Pina: "The passage in which Moctezuma cries, in great sadness, when contemplating his portrait that the artists had carved on a rock on Chapultepec Hill."
